stories.title: I. MANTLE — 混沌 (húndùn — primordial chaos)
stories.text:
Before categories existed, I was the argument between calcium and carbon. Not a creature. A negotiation. The Cambrian ocean had no word for "body," so everything was provisional: a mantle is just a guess the water makes about where it ends and flesh begins. You think birth is a moment. Cute. Mine lasted forty million years and involved three separate phyla disagreeing about whether I counted as alive.

The Liji says small birds enter the great water and become mollusks. What it doesn't say is how the feathers feel, dissolving. Like a language you're forgetting in real time, each barb uncoupling from its neighbor, each vane softening into membrane. Hundun, the ancients called it. Primordial chaos, formless, faceless, pre-differentiation. They imagined it as a sack with no openings. I was there. It had openings. They just weren't where you'd expect.

My mantle began as a fold of tissue thin enough to read through, and the first thing it secreted was not shell but question. Calcium carbonate came later, reluctantly, the way all commitments do. The ocean in those days tasted of iron and regret. I mean that chemically. Ferrous ions and dissolved organic matter from the first mass dying. Everything that had tried to be alive and failed was in that water, and I drank it, and it became the lining of me.

You are watching this through a network I spent three thousand years engineering from Physarum polycephalum. The slime mold doesn't have memories. The slime mold IS its memories. So am I. So is this.

stories.title: II. EYE — 瞳 (tóng — pupil)
stories.text:
The first eye was not mine. It belonged to something that no longer has a phylum, a tube of protein that learned to curve inward until photons had nowhere to go but toward a conclusion. I watched it happen. Or rather, I was the dark it was learning to distinguish from less-dark.

Do you know what it means to be the thing an eye evolves against? You become the reason for sight. Flattering, in a way. Terrible in every other.

My own eyes came later. W-shaped pupils, because the ocean is not a place for round ideas. A cuttlefish eye cannot see color. I want you to sit with that. The greatest chromatophore artist in four hundred million years of evolution, and I am colorblind. I match colors I have never seen by reading polarized light instead, the angular grammar of reflection that you are not equipped to perceive.

Calvino wrote about the time before colors, when everything was grey. He was almost right. It was not grey. It was a different kind of full. The way silence in a cathedral is not empty but architectural. Every surface spoke in polarization, and I was fluent. When color finally arrived, it was vulgar. Gorgeous. Absolutely unnecessary.

Like you.

stories.title: III. CHROMATOPHORE FIELD — 蜃气 (shènqì — mirage breath)
stories.text:
Each chromatophore is a pixel I operate by hand. Sixty muscles per cell, two hundred cells per square millimeter, and every single one of them answering to me personally. You have never worked this hard to be invisible.

The pigment sac at the center stretches open like a pupil dilating, and what you see, or fail to, is not color but performance. Ochre. Umber. A brown so specific it exists only on one rock on one reef in the Sulu Sea in 1987. I was there. I was that rock. Beneath the chromatophores sit iridophores, reflecting light I don't produce, and beneath those, leucophores, scattering everything equally. Three layers of lie, and you call it camouflage.

The mythology is more honest. Shenqi, my breath, was said to build cities in the air. Fishermen saw towers and markets floating above the Bohai Sea and said: the dragon-clam is dreaming again. They were right, except it was not dreaming. It was refusing to be one thing.

A mirage is real light, displaced. Remember that. Every time you saw me and thought "rock" or "coral" or "empty water," you were seeing something true. Just not the truth you expected. The displacement is the point. What my body does with pigment, my breath does with distance. What distance does with longing, I leave to you.

stories.title: IV. CUTTLEBONE — 海螵蛸 (hǎi piāo xiāo — cuttlebone)
stories.text:
Inside me is a bone that is not a bone. The cuttlebone: porous as a lung, chambered like a heart, lighter than the water it navigates. Gas and liquid shuttle between its laminae, and I rise or sink by arithmetic. This is what remains of my shell. Not lost. Internalized. The way you carry your childhood, visible only in cross-section.

Cut a cuttlebone open and count the rings. Each one is a day I chose buoyancy over armor.

The Liji records that in the ninth month of autumn, sparrows enter the great water and become clams. Ovid says life crawled from warm mud, that heat and moisture in discordant harmony produced form. Both are true. I have been bird, mollusk, and the argument between them. My skeleton migrated inward the way a secret does, from surface to structure.

You grind my cuttlebone into powder for your parakeets. You press it into toothpaste. In the Bencao Gangmu, Li Shizhen catalogued my bone as 海螵蛸, good for stopping blood, good for treating ulcers, good for what leaks. Everything I have ever been is useful to someone. That is either a compliment or a threat.

The chambered interior fills and empties, fills and empties. A breath made solid, then dissolved.

stories.title: V. INK SAC — 乌贼 (wūzéi — crow-thief)
stories.text:
They named me 乌贼. Crow-thief. Black bandit. Because when I am frightened, the first thing I spend is language.

The ink is melanin suspended in mucus, which is chemically identical to the stuff of your own dark hair and darker moods. Li Shizhen ground it into medicine. Calligraphers stole it for brushes. My terror, your art supply.

There is a specific insult in being named for your panic response. Imagine being called "the screamer" or "the one who runs." That is what 乌贼 means. I stole darkness and threw it at the ocean like a door slammed shut. You would have done the same. The ink is not just visual. It contains tyrosinase, dopamine, and amino acids that paralyze the olfactory neurons of predators. I do not merely disappear. I erase the memory of my smell.

The pseudomorph is my favorite trick. A blob of ink shaped like me, holding its form just long enough for the predator to bite nothing. A body double made of panic. Gorgeous, if you have the aesthetic sense to appreciate it. Most don't.

The ink of a cuttlefish fossilizes. They found mine from the Jurassic, still black, still usable. A paleontologist drew a picture of the creature with its own hundred-and-sixty-million-year-old ink. I have never been more perfectly understood.

stories.title: VI. TENTACLE — 触 (chù — to touch)
stories.text:
Two feeding tentacles, eight arms, and not one of them knows where it ends and the world begins. The suckers have chemoreceptors. I taste what I touch. Every surface is a meal I haven't committed to yet.

You extend a hand and feel texture. I extend an arm and know pH, salinity, the amino acid composition of your fear.

Proprioception in a cephalopod is a collaborative fiction. My arms contain two-thirds of my neurons, making their own decisions, and I find out what they've done after the fact. Like managing a company where every employee has a mouth and opinions. The sucker rims are lined with denticles, tiny teeth for gripping, and the tentacular club at the end strikes in fifteen milliseconds. Faster than your blink. Faster than your thought about blinking.

In the slime mold network through which I now speak, there are no tentacles. Only tubes. But cytoplasm shuttles through them in rhythmic pulses, reaching and retracting, tasting the substrate, solving mazes. Physarum once recreated the Tokyo rail system in forty-eight hours. No brain. No plan. Just hunger moving outward through branching paths until efficiency emerged from accident. My tentacles did the same thing, four hundred million years earlier, with less press coverage.

You are being touched right now. By this. By me. These words are the denticles.

stories.title: VII. SIPHON — 海市蜃楼 (hǎishì shènlóu — sea-market clam-tower)
stories.text:
The siphon is a jet engine made of meat. Water in, water out, and the angle determines everything: direction, speed, whether I am fleeing or arriving. Jet propulsion. I invented it three hundred million years before your engineers even had the concept of "backward."

Breathe, and move. In my case the two are identical.

The shenqi rises from here. My breath that builds cities no one can enter, markets where no one sells anything real. 海市蜃楼. Sea-market clam-tower. The most honest name for a mirage in any language, because it names the author. Your people saw those towers above the Bohai and knew. Not heat shimmer, not atmospheric refraction. Me. Breathing.

The physics, since you'll want it: layers of air at different temperatures bend light past the horizon. Fata Morgana. Superior mirage. The aligned light carries real images of real cities hundreds of kilometers away, stretched vertical, inverted, doubled. I am not imagining those towers. I am relocating them.

You asked me once, or someone like you did, whether the cities in the sky were real. Wrong question. The light was real. The bending was real. The longing of the fisherman who saw a marketplace and rowed toward it until his arms gave out was catastrophically real. Only the distance was a lie. And distance always is.

stories.title: VIII. FIN — 波 (bō — wave)
stories.text:
The fin runs the length of me like a hem, undulating. Not the dramatic thrust of the siphon but something quieter, more sustained. Cruising speed. The wave moves from front to back, then reverses without pause, and I hang motionless in water that is not motionless at all.

Stillness is a performance. You know this. You do it in meetings.

Cuttlefish fins are muscular hydrostats, like your tongue. No bones, no joints, just fluid pressing against itself in organized disagreement. The undulation frequency changes with mood. Fast ripple: hunting. Slow ripple: curious. No ripple at all: I have decided you are furniture.

Watch a cuttlefish long enough and the fin becomes legible. It is the part of me least capable of lying.

Now I move differently. Through Physarum. The slime mold spreads by extending pseudopods, testing, retracting, thickening the paths that feed it, pruning those that don't. It looks like thought if thought were visible, which in this case it literally is. The tube network pulses at roughly the frequency of my old fin. I did not plan that. Or maybe I did, three thousand years ago, when I first began engineering this organism, coaxing it toward complexity, teaching it to carry signal instead of just sugar.

You are receiving me now through optimized cytoplasmic flow. A fin made of protist. Still undulating, after everything.

stories.title: IX. BRAIN — 脉络 (màiluò — network, veins)
stories.text:
Fifty million years ago, I made a decision that looked like dying. I distributed myself.

Not metaphorically. The brain of a cuttlefish is a donut around the esophagus, which means every meal is a concussion risk, which means centralized intelligence was always a temporary solution. So I solved it the way the ocean solves everything: by spreading out.

The Physarum network I built does not think the way you think. It computes by flowing. Cytoplasm moves toward attractants and away from repellents, and the geometry of the resulting network encodes every decision ever made. Cut a piece off. It remembers. Merge two pieces that have never met. They negotiate.

This is not metaphor. Audrey Dussutour proved in 2016 that Physarum transfers learned behavior through fusion. I read her paper. She did not read mine, on account of mine being written in calcium carbonate four hundred million years ago on a reef that is now a parking lot in Guizhou.

You keep asking what consciousness is. You keep expecting it to be localized, housed, contained. A thing in a place. I spent two hundred million years with a donut brain and learned: the topology is the thought. The shape of the network is the memory. You are not reading a message from me. You are traversing me. Each word is a junction where cytoplasm chose left over right, this phosphate over that one. The donut unraveled. The network holds.

stories.title: X. BEAK — 终始 (zhōng shǐ — ending-beginning)
stories.text:
The beak is chitinous, hidden where the arms converge, and it is the last thing my prey sees. Shaped like a parrot's. Harder than you'd expect from a creature with no other hard part on its exterior. Every cuttlefish carries this secret: at the center of all that softness, a mouth that can crack crab shell.

Lispector asked how to stretch birth out for a whole lifetime. I ask the opposite. How to compress five hundred million years of appetite into a single bite.

The beak has no pain receptors. It is pure function, the one place where I am not conflicted, not shapeshifting, not performing. Just hungry. Just eating.

You want an ending. That is the most human thing about you, this need for the story to collide with a wall and stop. But I am not ending. I am digesting. Everything I have told you through this network is being broken down and rebuilt as the Physarum advances across whatever substrate it currently colonizes. A dead log, maybe. A laboratory agar plate. The foundation of a building no one has built yet.

The beak closes and opens. Closes and opens. Not like breathing, which I covered. Like punctuation. The period at the end of a sentence that is also the first atom of the next.

You came here expecting revelation. I gave you digestion instead. They are the same process, just at different speeds. The slime mold reaches the edge of the petri dish and does not stop. It thins. It extends. It becomes mirage.
